text:
Statement against arbitrary content takedown and account restrictions faced by public representatives and journalists

Earlier today, @Meta restricted the Instagram accounts (“Platform”) of @AamAadmiParty (AAP), its national convener @ArvindKejriwal, and Mohammed Zubair (@zoo_bear), co-founder of @AltNews. 

Over the past week, along with these instances, https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 has also recorded several instances of content takedowns faced by media organisations including @PeekTV_in, cartoonists such as @cartoonistrrs and @cartoonistvish, and @SauravDassss - @Cockroachisback's spokesperson.

According to the publicly available information, the affected posts were restricted pursuant to the “legal requests” received by the Platform. In many cases, users are provided little or no meaningful explanation about the legal or factual basis of the restriction or what steps they can take to challenge the decision. Such opaque moderation practices undermine users’ ability to understand how platform policies are enforced and make it difficult to distinguish between legitimate moderation and arbitrary or inconsistent decision-making. This is especially concerning where the affected content relates to political expression, criticism of public authorities, or peaceful protest, all of which occupy a central place in democratic discourse.

The Supreme Court of India upheld the constitutionality of Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000 (“IT Act”), on the basis that the statutory framework required that blocking orders be reasoned, necessary, and proportionate, and that such reasons must be recorded in writing to enable judicial review. By contrast, in most of these cases, notices sent to social media intermediaries through the Sahyog Portal under Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act and Rule 3(1)(d) of the IT Rules, 2021, leave users in the dark, with no recourse to meaningfully challenge takedowns and leave affected parties without legal redressal. The Sahyog Portal puts in place a parallel system to take down content online, without any of the safeguards present under Section 69A.

https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 has consistently advocated against these practices. We are concerned that this takedown drive is contrary to the rule of law and to India’s constitutional commitment to freedom of speech under Article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution.

While private platforms are not directly bound by the Constitution in the same manner as the State, their content moderation decisions increasingly influence the digital spaces in which democratic participation takes place. This places a heightened responsibility on platforms to ensure that their moderation processes are transparent, consistently applied, and accompanied by adequate procedural safeguards, including notice, reasons for enforcement actions, and effective mechanisms for review. At the same time, any direction issued by public authorities requiring platforms to restrict lawful online speech must comply with constitutional safeguards and the legal procedures prescribed under Indian law. Informal or opaque restrictions on political speech or press freedom undermine public trust and democratic accountability.

In light of the above, https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 calls for the following:

- Immediate disclosure of all takedown orders issued to platforms, including specific reasons and legal justifications.

- Strict adherence to the procedural safeguards laid out under Section 69A and the 2009 Blocking Rules, under the IT Act, which were upheld by the Supreme Court in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India.

- Notices received by social media intermediaries to be sent to every user affected to ensure transparency.

- Strengthening of independent oversight and appellate mechanisms to ensure that users can effectively challenge unlawful restrictions.

- Greater transparency from platforms regarding the number, nature, source, and outcome of governmental requests/orders for content removal and account restriction.

#freespeech #FoE #censorship #MetaCensorsIndia

text:
Statement: Proposed withdrawal of safe harbour under Section 79

5 November 2026

The Internet Freedom Foundation is alarmed by the Indian Express that the Ministry of Electronics and IT has begun discussions on stripping social media platforms of safe harbour under Section 79 of the IT Act, 2000. Nobody should mistake this for a move against Big Tech for it is a move against the people who use these platforms.

Safe harbour is not a gift to Meta, Google or X. It is the legal foundation that lets ordinary Indians speak online without a platform's lawyers deciding in advance whether their post is worth the risk and taking it down. If it is taken away, and every platform becomes liable for every post, comment and video. The rational response for any company is to remove anything that might draw a complaint, a notice or a summons. Criticism of the government, reporting on protests, satire, and the speech of people without lawyers will be the first casualties which are already being censored by automated filters implemented pursuant to the IT Rules, 2021. The Supreme Court recognised exactly this in Shreya Singhal (2015), which is why it read down Section 79(3)(b) to require a court order or a lawful government direction before platforms must act.

The timing tells its own story as the report says that MEITY’s rethink was shaped by a view within government that platform algorithms have favoured Opposition and anti-establishment narratives over official messaging, and by the role of Instagram during the student protests in July. In other words, the complaint is not that platforms host too much illegal content but it is that they host too much content the government dislikes. 

This is also the latest step in an escalation that has been building for years. The 2023 Fact Check Unit amendment tried to make the government the arbiter of truth about itself, until the Bombay High Court struck it down. The Sahyog portal has turned Section 79(3)(b) into a parallel, opaque takedown channel that sidesteps the safeguards of Section 69A, a practice X is now challenging in court. In August, a Parliamentary Standing Committee gave Mark Zuckerberg three days to apologise personally for the brief removal of the Prime Minister's video or face the loss of safe harbour. 

Subsequently advisories were issued on October 8, 2026 and October 10, 2026 pressuring digital platforms to implement pro-active censorship through, “enhanced due diligence”. Safe harbour was never meant to be a bargaining chip that MEITY waves at a company to extract compliance. 

There are real problems on these platforms such as child sexual abuse material, non-consensual intimate imagery and deepfakes. The Supreme Court's observations in Just Rights for Children Alliance on October 15 deserve a serious answer. But the answer is targeted, rights-respecting obligations with independent oversight, transparency about takedowns, and a grievance process that works for users. It is not a liability regime that pushes platforms to delete first and never ask. Nor is it a rule that platforms must clear product changes with the government before shipping them, which would hand the state a license raj over the design of the services Indians use every day.
Any change of this scale must go through Parliament, with a published draft, a genuine consultation and a full debate. It cannot be settled in closed-door meetings between the Ministry and a handful of companies.

What IFF will do

IFF will send a detailed representation to the Ministry of Electronics and IT setting out why the proposed changes to Section 79 are unconstitutional and unworkable, and what a rights-respecting approach to platform accountability should look like. We will also write to the Parliamentary Standing Committee on Communications and Information Technology.

We are filing RTI applications with MeitY seeking the minutes, agendas, attendance lists and file notings of every meeting held on the review of safe harbour, including the meetings with Meta and other platforms in July and August, and the basis for the Ministry's assessment of how platform algorithms treat government and Opposition content. The public has a right to know who is in the room when the rules of their speech are being rewritten.

We will publish what we receive, and we invite other civil society groups, journalists and platform users to join us in asking the Ministry to put any proposal to open consultation before it goes anywhere near Parliament.

text:
X is deeply concerned by the recent order from the Karnataka court in India, which will allow millions of police officers to issue arbitrary takedown orders through a secretive online portal called the Sahyog. This new regime has no basis in the law, circumvents Section 69A of the IT Act, violates Supreme Court rulings, and infringes Indian citizens’ constitutional rights to freedom of speech and expression. 

The Sahyog enables officers to order content removal based solely on allegations of “illegality,” without judicial review or due process for the speakers, and threatens platforms with criminal liability for non-compliance.

X respects and complies with Indian law, but this order fails to address the core constitutional issues in our challenge and is inconsistent with the Bombay High Court's recent ruling that a similar regime was unconstitutional. We respectfully disagree with the view that we have no right to raise these concerns because of our incorporation abroad—X contributes significantly to public discourse in India and the voice of our users is at the heart of our platform. We will appeal this order to defend free expression.

Statement : The removal of BitChat from the India App Store is unconstitutional. Section 69A permits the blocking of unlawful information, not of a messenger for working during internet shutdowns.

New Delhi, 3 October 2026

An Apple App Review notice published today by Jack Dorsey on X records that BitChat has been removed from the India App Store "per demand from the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology", issued under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, on the ground that the application "includes content that is illegal in India". The notice adds that BitChat's TestFlight builds are no longer available for testing in India. It does not identify the content said to be illegal or the ground under Section 69A invoked. The blocking order has not been published. The Internet Freedom Foundation condemns the order and calls for its immediate publication and withdrawal.

BitChat relays end-to-end encrypted messages between nearby phones over Bluetooth mesh. It has no servers and hosts no content of its own. What travels through it is the private speech of its users, so the claim that the application "includes" illegal content is incoherent. The State's actual objection stands recorded in the notices the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre issued on 23 July 2026 to GitHub, Google and Apple against BitChat, Briar and Bridgefy which stated that such applications work even during internet shutdowns and hamper lawful interception, attribution and traceability. Those notices, issued under Section 79(3)(b) were reportedly withdrawn after public disclosure. The same end has now been pursued through Section 69A. The objection is to capability of an application, not to content it transmits. A citizen's ability to speak to another citizen while the State has switched the internet off is not a ground of restriction under Section 69A or Article 19(2) of the Constitution.

Section 69A survived constitutional scrutiny in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) because of its safeguards which included the need for a reasoned, recorded order, committee review, and a hearing to the originator under Rule 8 of the Blocking Rules, 2009, which the Delhi High Court enforced in Tanul Thakur v. Union of India (2022). Further, Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020) requires that orders restricting fundamental rights be published and adopt the least restrictive measure. However, it appears in this instance, each safeguard has been evaded. A secret order blocking an entire application, rather than any identified unlawful information, is the most restrictive and disproprotionate measure available. Further, the confidentiality claimed under Rule 16 cannot defeat the right to challenge an order, and the constitutionality of this blocking regime is itself pending consideration before the Supreme Court.

While removal from the App Store does not delete BitChat from phones, it stops new downloads and security updates, leaving existing users on unpatched versions, and it ends security testing in India through TestFlight. During the Jantar Mantar protests, when mobile internet was suspended and jammers were deployed, Bluetooth mesh messaging was a channel of last resort through which young people coordinated their safety. To our knowledge, Apple has removed BitChat on a government's demand in only one other country. This is in China, in April this year.

Our demands

1. MeitY must publish the blocking order, the ground invoked and the record of the committee's proceedings, and serve the developers with a copy and an opportunity of hearing.

2. The direction must be withdrawn. Any specific unlawful use must be met with targeted proceedings under due process, not the removal of a communications tool for everyone.

3. Apple must disclose the demand in its transparency reporting and notify its users in India, and must state whether parallel directions have been received in respect of other app stores.

4. The secrecy of the blocking regime must end. The Blocking Rules, 2009 should be amended to require publication of orders and notice to originators, without awaiting the outcome of the pending constitutional challenge.

The Internet Freedom Foundation will file applications under the Right to Information Act seeking a copy of the order, and stands ready to assist the developers and affected users in India.

Statement on MeitY's notice to WhatsApp over the "usernames" feature

The Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) has sent WhatsApp a notice about the usernames feature it announced on 29 June 2026. The notice asks the company to explain, within three days, why regulatory action should not be taken against it "for launching a feature that may increase cybercrimes", and it directs the company "not to roll out this feature until the consultation on this point is achieved to the satisfaction of the Government". The Internet Freedom Foundation is concerned that the notice has no clear basis in law. It is an attempt by the executive to decide what a company may build and ship, which no statute permits.

The notice treats the launch of a lawful feature as a wrong the company must justify. That reverses the ordinary position especially given the absence of any clear legal power that exists. MeitY does not name any provision that lets it approve a product feature before release or order one withdrawn, because there is none, and the provisions it does cite do not supply that power.

Section 79 of the IT Act, 2000 is a safe harbour that protects an intermediary from liability for what its users post, so long as it observes due diligence. It decides when a platform can be held liable. It is not a power for MeitY to decide what features the platform may offer. Sections 66C and 66D punish identity theft and cheating by personation. They are criminal offences, tried by courts, aimed at the person who steals an identity, not at the maker of a tool that a third party misuses. Also, on MeitY's logic, a telecom operator could be told not to sell SIM cards because SIM cards are used in almost every online fraud. 

Rule 3(1)(b), Rule 3(2) and Rule 4 of the IT Rules, 2021 are due diligence and grievance obligations and cannot be converted into a licensing scheme. Section 69A, the one provision that lets MeitY control what appears online, permits the blocking of specific information through a set procedure. It says nothing about which features a company may build. Further the IT Rules, 2021 are subordinate legislation made under Sections 79 and 87 of the IT Act, and subordinate rules cannot travel beyond the parent statute (Ajoy Kumar Banerjee v. Union of India). If a rule cannot exceed the Act, a letter certainly cannot. The power to require prior permission for a feature is not in the Act, not in the Rules, and cannot be created by a notice. 

MeitY has tried this before. In March 2024 it told the same large intermediaries, among them AI Companies, to obtain its explicit permission before deploying under-tested AI models. That was criticised as an overreach that sought to build a licensing mechanism with no empowering provision in the IT Act, and within a fortnight MeitY withdrew it and dropped the permission requirement. This notice repeats the move for a single feature and goes further, because it names one company, sets a three-day clock, and bars the launch until MeitY is satisfied. 

This matters beyond WhatsApp. A power asserted against one company by letter can be turned on any company and any feature. On this reasoning MeitY could tell a browser not to switch on a privacy setting by default, or a payments app not to add a login method, each time until it was content. The notice also invokes traceability, through Rule 4(2) of the IT Rules, 2021 and the identification of the "first originator" of a message. Rule 4(2) has been challenged as exceeding its parent provision and resting on no law made by Parliament, and that challenge is pending before the Delhi High Court. Raising it against a feature meant to share fewer identifiers fits a pattern. 

We ask MeitY to state the exact provision of law under which this notice, and the direction to halt the roll-out, has been issued, and to withdraw that direction. It should stop using Section 79 and the contested traceability rule as leverage to control product design and to reverse features that improve privacy. Impersonation and fraud are real risks, but they are met by enforcing the criminal law against those who commit them, and by open processes that rest on identified legal powers. They are not met by MeitY deciding, in private and by letter, what features Indians may use. That is a licence raj for software features.

New Delhi, 1 July 2026

India’s Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MEITY), issued a blocking order against the bitchat Android app. Consequently, the app has been removed and is no longer available on Google Play for users in India. https://t.co/2euQCFXKth

Last night IFF, @SFLCin and @geoblockedindia received a legal notice said to be issued purportedly on behalf of the RSS. It’s hard to believe this comes from an organisation that has had a century to practise its paperwork and hence this may even be a weird prank! This notice asks us to stop criticising the Government’s blocking orders and stop documenting them. It also wants us to confirm in writing within seven days (seriously).

We can tell it’s an excellent teaching aid and here are seven lessons from it.

1) Say who you are: The notice names no advocate and gives no enrollment number. It is signed by an “Authorised Signatory” with no name. Replies go to a free Proton Mail ID, and the “office” is a residential flat in outer Delhi. A notice that can’t tell you who sent it is less a legal document than a weather event.

2) Have a grievance of your own: It never says how its client is harmed when we criticise a MeitY advisory. It complains on behalf of the Government’s blocking orders. The Union has no shortage of lawyers, and it hasn’t asked for volunteers.

3) Name the law: It threatens “appropriate legal action” under “the applicable provisions of law” and doesn’t cite a single section of any statute. A threat with no law, is literally an empty threat.

4) Don’t ask people to give up a fundamental right within seven days: The first demand is that we stop “publicly opposing” government directions. In Shreya Singhal (2015), the Supreme Court held that discussion and advocacy of a cause, however unpopular, sit at the heart of Article 19(1)(a). Opposing an order is how its legality gets tested. That is the Constitution working as intended.

5) Check whether the courts asked for the thing you want stopped” In Anuradha Bhasin (2020), the Supreme Court held that orders restricting fundamental rights must be made available so people can challenge them. The Reddit order is on the public Lumen Database because Reddit put it there. Reading a public database and saying what’s in it has a name. It’s called research.

6) Show us the spark and the powder keg: The notice says our work weakens national security measures, but it gives no instance, date or harm. In S. Rangarajan (1989), the Supreme Court held that the danger feared from speech can’t be remote, conjectural or far-fetched. It has to be like a spark in a powder keg. A post about a Lumen filing is not a spark.

7) Read it once more before you press send: The paragraphs run 1, then an empty 2 and 3, then 4. A PIN code wanders into the facts. The account it targets is on “Twitter”. 

Our reply is short. The notice is legally deficient because it makes no material allegation and cites no illegality. We will respectfully continue to advance constitutional rights, as we have done before. Notices like this rarely expect to win in court. They expect the recipient to get tired. We often are tired, but it has never changed what we do. Solidarity with @SFLCin and @geoblockedindia. 

If your post or account has been blocked in India, write to legal@internetfreedom.in.

A 2.6 million-view Instagram reel documenting the concerns of residents affected by a proposed Google data centre in Visakhapatnam was blocked in India without prior notice, a hearing, or a copy of the blocking order being provided to the journalists who made it. When the order was finally obtained through litigation, it referred to an entirely unrelated individual. IFF has now sought a review and restoration of the reel.
Read More: https://t.co/z4Ps7Umqrk

A shorter 2:01-minute version of their video report was specifically edited for Instagram. The reel went viral and received around 2.6 million views before it was blocked in India on 22 May 2026 under Section 79(3)(b) of the Information Technology Act, 2000. The journalists were not informed beforehand about the action. (3/7)

Shamsheer approached both MeitY and Meta seeking clarification, restoration of the reel, and a copy of the blocking order. Neither responded with the requested information. With no other meaningful avenue available, Shamsheer and Monica approached the Delhi High Court seeking the restoration of the reel and disclosure of the order behind its blocking. (4/7)

Muslim IT Cell (@Muslim_ITCell) has written to MeitY seeking a copy of the blocking order and its grounds, and plans to pursue legal action to challenge the restriction and seek restoration of its X account. https://t.co/7NoPYBts6w

The blocking of social media accounts citing Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act, 2000 is, in most if not all instances, being facilitated by the Sahyog Censorship Portal, first established through a MeitY Office Memorandum and subsequently formalised through amendments to the IT Rules, 2021 in Rule 3(1)(d). This portal is being provided by the Ministry of Home Affairs From our understanding and observed censorship trends, these Sahyog notices are being issued by at least 35 State Police Departments across the country who are, "nodal officers". See screenshot.

When a person's account is blocked, they typically receive inadequate information from the intermediary (Meta, Google, X), communications that merely cite Section 79(3)(b). X is not part of the Sahyog platform but is serviced through its own notification mechanism. Neither MeitY nor the police authority informs the user of the reasons for blocking, the date of the order, or the issuing authority. Hence, the first step for an affected party is therefore to write to MeitY and the intermediary requesting a copy of the order, since Rule 3(1)(d) of the IT Rules, 2021 imposes no confidentiality requirement. For the text of the rule, see screenshot.

Such requests are often refused, forcing affected users to approach a High Court first to obtain the order, and then, if it has been jurisdictionally issued in the same state where High Court proceedings are pending, to challenge it on merits. It is also unclear whether the review committees envisaged under Rule 3(1)(d) actually exist and their composition, contact details, and meeting dates are nowhere disclosed, leaving censored users without recourse.

This is a Kafkaesque system designed by MeitY and the MHA. It is the digital infrastructure of censorship under which users who criticise the government, comment on social and cultural issues, or opposition political parties are being silenced online. 

More information and analysis available here : https://t.co/XIVXL5WzI9

For any support or questions please always feel free email on legal@internetfreedom.in

Thank you to the amazing Gamban Team and its founders @mattzarb and Jack Symons for reposing faith in us. It’s one of the rare occasions where @GoI_MeitY has reversed its order of blocking content under Section 69A of the IT Act. Grateful to the Hon’ble Delhi High Court for its directions to MeitY & to the officials of MeitY & the Inter-Ministerial Committee for giving us a patient hearing & an opportunity to address all their concerns. @SecretaryMEITY

Statement : Shutting down Telegram is a band aid solution and is a disproportionate answer to exam fraud

The Internet Freedom Foundation objects to the directions announced today in the National Testing Agency's press release on action against the Telegram platform. On the NTA's recommendation, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology has, under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, restricted access to the whole of Telegram in India until 22 June 2026, and has separately ordered the platform to switch off message-editing for every Indian user until 30 June 2026. This is a blunt, nationwide measure aimed at the conduct of rampant fraud rackets, and on the Government's own admission is constitutionally incompatible.

At the outset it is important to note that Section 69A and the Blocking Rules of 2009 framed under it allow the Government to block access to specific “information” on a computer resource. They do not extend to switching off an entire intermediary, still less to ordering a company to redesign its product by removing a feature for a whole country. In Shreya Singhal v Union of India, the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A because it is narrow and hedged with procedural safeguards. Reading it to authorise shutting down a platform that lakhs use is an overbroad restriction by the NTAs own admission. For the message-editing direction the release identifies no source of power at all. If one exists, the order must say so.

The release argues against itself

A restriction on access has to be the least intrusive measure that achieves its aim as per the constitutional test of proportionality laid down in Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) and applied in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020). The NTA's own narration shows the block fails its nodal agency, the release says, “has secured the prompt take-down of a substantial number of Telegram channels, groups and bots”, and this targeted work “is the reason the harm caused by these rackets has been contained to the extent it has”. If channel level takedown contained the harm, the case for a blanket block collapses and hence the Government has reached for a heavier tool while conceding that a lighter one was working. The collateral cost sits on the record too as noted in the press release. The block, the NTA accepts, “affects lakhs of citizens who use the Telegram platform for legitimate personal, educational, professional and informational purposes”. The release also says there is "no such paper available outside the secured examination chain" and that “the security of the examination is unaffected by the action taken”. If the exam is secure and no leak exists, what is being suppressed is rumour, and rumour cannot justify closing a platform when specific blocking and criminal prosecution remain available.

Students use of Telegram

The block of telegram is reactive and ineffective and will punish ordinary users instead of addressing the systemic source of exam leaks. This blocking comes in the final days of NEET preparation, when thousands of students depend on Telegram for study groups, doubt-clearing, and shared resources. Also, it is important to consider that the source of exam papers leak will occur from inside the system, among insiders and across the printing and logistics chain, with the platform being the most downstream channel for distribution. Hence, switching off Telegram, is merely a deflection from the repeated failures that will continue while media attention is directed towards this Telegram ban.

Lack of transparency

At present only a press release from the NTA has been provided, which recommended the block but the reasoned order of MeitY, the authority that issued it, has not been released. The Anuradha Bhasin decision requires that orders restricting access be published so they can be tested in court. Here the order, and the reasoning of the committee behind it, stay out of view, and we do not know whether Telegram was heard at all. An announcement of a block is no substitute for an order the affected party can challenge.
Blunt to enforce and very easy to evade
Usually, app-level blocks run through IS-level DNS and IP filtering. They are over inclusive, sweeping in lawful use, yet simple to evade as a determined exam leak racket moves to a VPN or a mirror within minutes while ordinary users lose the service for a week.

We ask the Government to:

1) Publish the MeitY Section 69A order and the NTA recommendation behind it, with reasons;
2) State the legal basis for the message editing direction, or withdraw it;
3) Confirm whether Telegram was given a hearing under the Blocking Rules, and place the committee's record before any court that hears a challenge; and
4) Lift the platform-wide restriction and rely on the targeted takedowns the NTA itself credits with containing the harm.

We emphasise that the NEET (UG) 2026 re-examination is worth protecting and it concerns the future of lakhs of aspirants. It requires securing the entire process of examination rather than reaching for purported band aid solutions that instead cause more harm. The State cannot switch off a service used by lakhs to answer the wrongdoing of a few, and cannot do it through an order no one affected is allowed to read. On its own facts, the Government has done both.

New Delhi, 16 June 2026.

WHY ARE SOCIAL MEDIA TAKEDOWNS IN FOCUS?

Introduction

Increasing content takedowns expose the tension between digital governance and constitutional freedoms, raising concerns over censorship, intermediary accountability and procedural safeguards in India's evolving digital democracy.

Main Facts

🌟 Recent Trigger: MeitY advisories dated October 8 and 10, 2026, directed platforms to address misleading content, AI-generated deepfakes and public-order concerns.

🌟 IT Act, 2000: Section 69A empowers the government to block online information on specified grounds, including sovereignty, security and public order.

🌟 Intermediary Liability: Section 79 provides conditional safe-harbour protection to platforms hosting third-party content.

🌟 IT Rules, 2021: Rule 3(1)(d) governs removal following legally qualifying court orders or authorised-government notifications.

🌟 Accelerated Compliance: The 2026 amendments reportedly reduce the takedown compliance window from 36 hours to three hours in specified cases.

🌟 Judicial Safeguard: Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) restricted intermediary takedown obligations to legally recognised actual knowledge.

Challenges

🌟 Free-Speech Erosion: Arbitrary restrictions can undermine Article 19(1)(a), subject to Article 19(2).

🌟 Executive Overreach: Broad advisories risk excessive discretionary censorship.

🌟 Algorithmic Opacity: Automated moderation may suppress legitimate political discourse.

🌟 Due-Process Deficit: Delayed appeals and inadequate explanations weaken accountability.

🌟 Digital Exclusion: Account restrictions can damage livelihoods, reputation and access to information.

Constructive Criticism

🌟 Combating misinformation is legitimate, but national security cannot become a blanket justification for censorship. Proportionality and transparency are indispensable.

Way Forward

🌟 Ensure reasoned, narrowly tailored blocking orders.

🌟 Strengthen independent oversight and judicial review.

🌟 Provide timely appeals, user notification and transparency reports.

🌟 Adopt risk-based AI-content labelling and human review.

🌟 Protect lawful criticism and journalistic expression.

Highlighted Keywords

Digital Constitutionalism, Safe Harbour, Prior Restraint, Procedural Due Process, Algorithmic Accountability.

Conclusion

A democratic state must regulate digital harm without regulating dissent; constitutional liberty must remain the cornerstone of digital governance.

text:
WHEN A CREATOR SPEAKS UP, DOES HER VOICE BECOME THE TARGET? DIGITAL CENSORSHIP, META RESTRICTIONS AND THE RIGHT TO BE HEARD

A creator behind @the.ranting.gola has shared a disturbing account of restrictions on her Facebook activity. In her video, she says she cannot go LIVE for a year, send messages, post videos to her broadcast group or share videos to her Story. She also describes monetisation being unavailable and some content becoming inaccessible in India.

She says she had made a video supporting Neha Singh Rathore and opposing ABVP-related groups. According to her account, she was not clearly informed which specific post had triggered the restrictions and had to investigate the matter herself.

These are the creator’s allegations and account of her experience. The precise reason for the restrictions, the applicable Meta policy and whether a government direction was involved have not been independently established from this video alone.

But her experience raises a fundamental democratic question: What happens when ordinary citizens and independent creators lose their ability to communicate with their audiences without receiving a clear explanation?

THIS IS NOT AN ISOLATED CONCERN

Recent reporting in India makes these questions particularly urgent.

• ThePrint, 19 October 2026: Reported on a MeitY advisory asking Meta to review its Facebook and Instagram recommendation systems, alongside restrictions affecting posts and accounts connected with protests and political events.

https://t.co/QeWUIIrGmC

• Alt News, 15 October 2026: Documented restrictions affecting journalists and media organisations covering the Delhi protests, including cases in which Meta notices cited automated enforcement or government and law-enforcement requests.

https://t.co/1RjkoJX1nE

• Reporters Without Borders: Reported a broader rise in restrictions affecting journalistic content in India during 2026, raising concerns about opaque takedown processes and the public’s right to information.

https://t.co/g6FhmAUglC

These reports provide important context. They do not, by themselves, establish that this particular creator was restricted at the government's request. That question deserves a direct, evidence-based answer.

THE REAL ISSUE: TRANSPARENCY AND ACCOUNTABILITY

Social media companies have the right to enforce legitimate community standards. But enforcement must be proportionate, transparent and open to meaningful appeal.

If a creator is prohibited from going LIVE for an entire year, the platform should explain:

Which specific post, video or action triggered the restriction?
Which rule was allegedly violated, and what evidence supports that decision?
Was the action taken under Meta's own policies, an automated system or a government/legal request?
Why were such extensive restrictions imposed, and what appeal and restoration mechanisms are available?

A vague account-status notification is not an adequate substitute for a meaningful explanation.

DEMOCRACY CANNOT BE MEASURED ONLY BY ELECTIONS

Democracy also depends on the freedom to question power, criticise political organisations, support dissenting voices and share information without arbitrary punishment.

When restrictions disproportionately affect people discussing political controversies, the public deserves to know whether the cause is legitimate policy enforcement, automated error, coordinated reporting or an external legal direction. These possibilities must be investigated rather than assumed.

Our demand is simple: transparency from Meta, accountability from any authority that seeks unlawful restrictions, and equal protection for every citizen's right to express a political opinion.

No creator should have to guess why their voice has been restricted. No government should be allowed to silence lawful criticism through opaque processes. And no technology company should be permitted to hide consequential decisions behind unexplained notifications.

If the restrictions were justified, publish the reasons. If they were mistaken or unlawful, restore the affected rights. Let evidence decide—not political loyalty.

Statement : The blocking of BitChat's code on GitHub is unconstitutional and authoritarian. 

New Delhi, 24 July 2026

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) condemns the order issued by the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C), Ministry of Home Affairs, directing GitHub to remove the code repositories of BitChat. 

The order, Notice No. 11072601011432, was issued at 11:16 pm on 23 July 2026 under Section 79(3)(b) of the Information Technology Act, 2000 read with Rule 3(1)(d) of the IT Rules, 2021. The order directs GitHub to disable access to three repositories, including the Android application and its release files, within three hours. It threatens the platform with loss of safe harbour and criminal prosecution. No copy was published by the Government of India. The public learnt of it from a post by @jack, whose team develops BitChat. Censorship in India now comes to light through disclosure by the censored.

Since 17 July 2026, the Ministry of Home Affairs has suspended mobile internet around Jantar Mantar as per public reports about five times, most recently within a 1.5 kilometre radius from 4 pm until midnight on 23 July. That radius takes in Janpath and parts of Connaught Place. Reports describe signal jammers at the protest site and people walking two kilometres before their phones work. Inside that zone a student separated from her group during a detention drive cannot send a message to say where she is. Thousands of students and young people have camped at Jantar Mantar since June, seeking accountability for examination irregularities. Permission for their march to Parliament was refused. Metro stations were shut and also internet connectivity has been blocked.

BitChat is an open source application built for exactly this situation. It passes messages from phone to phone over Bluetooth, without mobile networks or a central server. It is striking that the order does not identify a single unlawful message. It objects to what BitChat is. In its own words, the application is dangerous because it enables communication "even during network restrictions" and can "circumvent lawful restrictions" during "internet shutdowns". Hence, the government's objection is that citizens can speak to one another while it has switched the internet off. 

The order is illegal on at least four grounds. 

1. Section 79(3)(b) is not a blocking power. In Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) 5 SCC 1, the Supreme Court read down the provision. Intermediaries may be required to act only on a court order, or a government notification confined to the grounds under Article 19(2) of the Constitution. Blocking is governed exclusively by Section 69A and the Blocking Rules, 2009, which require a hearing and reasons recorded in writing, subject to review. Directions issued under Section 79(3)(b), Rule 3(1)(d) and the Sahyog Portal evade these safeguards, and constitutional challenges to this parallel regime are pending before High Courts. 

2. The reasons in the order are circular. The order asserts that the repositories contain "information which is prohibited under any law" without naming any such information, and rests on what the application is "capable of" enabling. Anticipated misuse of a communications tool is not a lawful basis to prohibit the tool. By this logic a telephone exchange could be sealed. 

3. The order cites Section 43 of the IT Act, a civil compensation provision, alongside conspiracy and abetment offences under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, against a platform that hosts code. 

4. A three hour deadline issued close to midnight forecloses legal assessment and recourse, and fails the proportionality standard in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020) 3 SCC 637.

The order also fails on its own terms as deleting a repository does not delete the application from any phone that carries it, and the mesh keeps functioning without servers. What the takedown actually prevents is scrutiny of the underlying code.

IFF demands that the Government of India:

1. Withdraw Notice No. 11072601011432 dated 23 July 2026 issued to GitHub.
2. Publish every takedown direction issued under Section 79(3)(b), Rule 3(1)(d) and the Sahyog Portal, with the reasons recorded for each.
3. Restore full connectivity around Jantar Mantar, publish all suspension orders, and disclose the legal authority for the deployment of jammers.

We stand with the developers and the young protesters whose speech this order seeks to silence.

Statement: Proposed withdrawal of safe harbour under Section 79

5 November 2026

The Internet Freedom Foundation is alarmed by the Indian Express that the Ministry of Electronics and IT has begun discussions on stripping social media platforms of safe harbour under Section 79 of the IT Act, 2000. Nobody should mistake this for a move against Big Tech for it is a move against the people who use these platforms.

Safe harbour is not a gift to Meta, Google or X. It is the legal foundation that lets ordinary Indians speak online without a platform's lawyers deciding in advance whether their post is worth the risk and taking it down. If it is taken away, and every platform becomes liable for every post, comment and video. The rational response for any company is to remove anything that might draw a complaint, a notice or a summons. Criticism of the government, reporting on protests, satire, and the speech of people without lawyers will be the first casualties which are already being censored by automated filters implemented pursuant to the IT Rules, 2021. The Supreme Court recognised exactly this in Shreya Singhal (2015), which is why it read down Section 79(3)(b) to require a court order or a lawful government direction before platforms must act.

The timing tells its own story as the report says that MEITY’s rethink was shaped by a view within government that platform algorithms have favoured Opposition and anti-establishment narratives over official messaging, and by the role of Instagram during the student protests in July. In other words, the complaint is not that platforms host too much illegal content but it is that they host too much content the government dislikes. 

This is also the latest step in an escalation that has been building for years. The 2023 Fact Check Unit amendment tried to make the government the arbiter of truth about itself, until the Bombay High Court struck it down. The Sahyog portal has turned Section 79(3)(b) into a parallel, opaque takedown channel that sidesteps the safeguards of Section 69A, a practice X is now challenging in court. In August, a Parliamentary Standing Committee gave Mark Zuckerberg three days to apologise personally for the brief removal of the Prime Minister's video or face the loss of safe harbour. 

Subsequently advisories were issued on October 8, 2026 and October 10, 2026 pressuring digital platforms to implement pro-active censorship through, “enhanced due diligence”. Safe harbour was never meant to be a bargaining chip that MEITY waves at a company to extract compliance. 

There are real problems on these platforms such as child sexual abuse material, non-consensual intimate imagery and deepfakes. The Supreme Court's observations in Just Rights for Children Alliance on October 15 deserve a serious answer. But the answer is targeted, rights-respecting obligations with independent oversight, transparency about takedowns, and a grievance process that works for users. It is not a liability regime that pushes platforms to delete first and never ask. Nor is it a rule that platforms must clear product changes with the government before shipping them, which would hand the state a license raj over the design of the services Indians use every day.
Any change of this scale must go through Parliament, with a published draft, a genuine consultation and a full debate. It cannot be settled in closed-door meetings between the Ministry and a handful of companies.

What IFF will do

IFF will send a detailed representation to the Ministry of Electronics and IT setting out why the proposed changes to Section 79 are unconstitutional and unworkable, and what a rights-respecting approach to platform accountability should look like. We will also write to the Parliamentary Standing Committee on Communications and Information Technology.

We are filing RTI applications with MeitY seeking the minutes, agendas, attendance lists and file notings of every meeting held on the review of safe harbour, including the meetings with Meta and other platforms in July and August, and the basis for the Ministry's assessment of how platform algorithms treat government and Opposition content. The public has a right to know who is in the room when the rules of their speech are being rewritten.

We will publish what we receive, and we invite other civil society groups, journalists and platform users to join us in asking the Ministry to put any proposal to open consultation before it goes anywhere near Parliament.

WHY ARE SOCIAL MEDIA TAKEDOWNS IN FOCUS?

Introduction

Increasing content takedowns expose the tension between digital governance and constitutional freedoms, raising concerns over censorship, intermediary accountability and procedural safeguards in India's evolving digital democracy.

Main Facts

🌟 Recent Trigger: MeitY advisories dated October 8 and 10, 2026, directed platforms to address misleading content, AI-generated deepfakes and public-order concerns.

🌟 IT Act, 2000: Section 69A empowers the government to block online information on specified grounds, including sovereignty, security and public order.

🌟 Intermediary Liability: Section 79 provides conditional safe-harbour protection to platforms hosting third-party content.

🌟 IT Rules, 2021: Rule 3(1)(d) governs removal following legally qualifying court orders or authorised-government notifications.

🌟 Accelerated Compliance: The 2026 amendments reportedly reduce the takedown compliance window from 36 hours to three hours in specified cases.

🌟 Judicial Safeguard: Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) restricted intermediary takedown obligations to legally recognised actual knowledge.

Challenges

🌟 Free-Speech Erosion: Arbitrary restrictions can undermine Article 19(1)(a), subject to Article 19(2).

🌟 Executive Overreach: Broad advisories risk excessive discretionary censorship.

🌟 Algorithmic Opacity: Automated moderation may suppress legitimate political discourse.

🌟 Due-Process Deficit: Delayed appeals and inadequate explanations weaken accountability.

🌟 Digital Exclusion: Account restrictions can damage livelihoods, reputation and access to information.

Constructive Criticism

🌟 Combating misinformation is legitimate, but national security cannot become a blanket justification for censorship. Proportionality and transparency are indispensable.

Way Forward

🌟 Ensure reasoned, narrowly tailored blocking orders.

🌟 Strengthen independent oversight and judicial review.

🌟 Provide timely appeals, user notification and transparency reports.

🌟 Adopt risk-based AI-content labelling and human review.

🌟 Protect lawful criticism and journalistic expression.

Highlighted Keywords

Digital Constitutionalism, Safe Harbour, Prior Restraint, Procedural Due Process, Algorithmic Accountability.

Conclusion

A democratic state must regulate digital harm without regulating dissent; constitutional liberty must remain the cornerstone of digital governance.

April 4, 2026 | New Delhi: The Editors Guild of India is deeply concerned by both the contents and the underlying intent behind the Draft Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Second Amendment Rules, 2026 (“Draft Amendments”), which were made public by the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) on March 30, 2026, with just a fortnight given for comments.
Prima facie, the amended rules and guidelines, whose stated purpose is to “strengthen compliance” and increase the effectiveness of regulatory oversight of content regulation mechanisms under Part III (Code of Ethics relating to Digital Media) of the IT Rules, 2021” appear to arm MeitY with sweeping powers of content regulation, sharply increases the compliance burden on digital intermediaries, and gives the executive overarching powers to block or take down content generated by  “non news publishers” and intermediaries. This will directly infringe the fundamental right to free speech guaranteed to all citizens under the Constitution and will have a chilling effect on freedom of expression and the airing of contrarian views, which are fundamental to an open and functional democracy.
Sub-rule (4) to Rule 3, which deals with due diligence obligations of intermediaries, now makes it mandatory on the part of intermediaries to comply with “any clarification, advisory, order, direction, standard operating procedure, code of practice or guideline issued by the ministry, by order in writing”. Failure to comply has been linked to loss of the safe harbour protection extended to intermediaries and platforms for user-generated content, under section 79 of the Information Technology Act. The absence of due process for the issuance of compliance orders and the complete lack of transparency in the process are deeply concerning.
Changes to Rule 14(2) and Rule 14(5) in the draft amendment also greatly widen the powers of the Inter-Departmental Committee (IDC). IDC, a central oversight body constituted under Rule 14 of the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021, was specifically created to hear grievances and complaints against digital content. Now, the IDC has been empowered to deal with and “matter” – a generalisation which arms the body to consider virtually any issue, in the absence of any definition of what constitutes a “matter”. Other provisions devolve rulemaking powers entirely to the executive branch, removing the window for legislative oversight provided under the IT Act.
The EGi calls on the government to urgently review or recall the draft rules, and engage in more constructive consultations with all sections of stakeholders and take on board valid concerns and objections.
Warm regards,
Sanjay Kapoor, President
Raghavan Srinivasan, General Secretary
Teresa Rehman, Treasurer

MeitY has invited stakeholder comments on the Draft amendments to Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021. The deadline to submit comments is 14th April 2026.

The proposed amendments are a significant enhancement of the Government's powers. They propose to,

(a)  Significantly expand the role of the Ministerial level Inter-Departmental Committee (IDC) to hear matters beyond the violation of the Code of Ethics set out in Part III of the IT Rules, as may be referred to the IDC by the MIB. This also expands the MIB's power to interdict online content, including news, since the proposed amendment significantly broadens the scope of matters the MIB can refer to the IDC, which is empowered to issue a recommendation to the MIB. 
(b) Expands and proposes to apply the Code of Ethics and compliance as directed by the IDC to intermediaries. The Code of Ethics was earlier limited to News Publishers and Online Curated Content Publishers.
(c)  Expands Intermediary Due Diligence compliance requirements by requiring compliance with MeitY’s advisories, directions, SOPs, Guidelines, etc., as part of the Intermediary Due Diligence obligations. 
(d) Clarifies that the record retention obligations under the IT Rules are in addition to requirements under other laws.

As AI becomes part of India’s critical infrastructure, questions around accountability, data privacy and responsible use are becoming increasingly important. TRAI has released draft guidelines for the responsible use of AI in telecom networks, while MeitY’s new handbook on the Data Empowerment and Protection Architecture (DEPA) outlines how institutions can collaborate on AI training while retaining control over their datasets.

Alongside these efforts, DataDaan, a voluntary initiative by https://t.co/NhxaUPXSIt and the Centre for Policy Research and Governance (CPRG), invites individuals and organisations to pledge legally compliant, non-personal datasets for developing AI solutions that address Indian needs.

Is India Becoming an AI Data Colony?

Every time you post a photo on Instagram, update your job history on LinkedIn, or share your thoughts on Twitter, you are leaving a digital footprint. 

Right now, Large Language Models (LLMs) are vacuuming up this exact data to train their systems.

These AI giants aren't just reading classic literature. 

They are ingesting your public conversations, your preferences, and your personal milestones. Because this data is technically "public," tech companies treat your digital life as free real estate.

This is where geography starts to dictate your rights. 

In the European Union, data laws enforce strict boundaries. Tech platforms operating in the EU are required to offer citizens clear "opt-out" mechanisms before their personal data can be fed into an AI training model.

In India, the reality is much different. 

We have the Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Act of 2023, which is currently being implemented in phases through 2026. While the act establishes a consent framework, publicly available social media data often falls into a massive gray area.

Without mandatory, easy-to-use opt-out features for AI training, we risk returning to a colonial dynamic. 

Foreign tech giants get to extract the raw material—our billions of digital footprints—refine it, and sell the resulting AI products back to us.

This directly threatens the spirit of the landmark 2017 Supreme Court judgment that recognized the Right to Privacy as a fundamental right. 

Privacy is not just about hiding secrets; it is about having autonomy over how your identity is used, commodified, and monetized.

So, what can you do to protect your digital legacy?

First, audit your platform settings. Lock down personal accounts where possible. Even though it is often buried deep in the privacy menus, manually toggle off data-sharing for AI training on any platform that offers the option.

Second, be deeply intentional about your public footprint. Stop oversharing sensitive personal milestones on public feeds, watermark your original visual or written work, and start treating your online presence as a highly valuable asset—because to the AI industry, it already is.

Compliance with India's data privacy act (DPDP Act) is no longer something organizations can put off.

कुछ दिन पहले ही Facebook ने मेरे “Ambuj Kumar – Lokhit India” पेज को डीमोनेटाइज कर दिया था। शिकायत करने और सवाल उठाने के बाद मोनेटाइजेशन बहाल हुआ। अब आज, 9 नवंबर 2026 को, इसी नाम वाले अकाउंट पर भारत में 7 दिन की रोक की सूचना मिली है। पेज, वीडियो और फोटो तक पहुंच प्रतिबंधित करने के अलग संदेश भी आए हैं।

Facebook इन कार्रवाइयों के लिए “भारत सरकार/कानून लागू करने वाली एजेंसी” के नोटिस और स्थानीय कानूनों का हवाला दे रहा है। संदेशों में IT Act की धारा 79(3)(b) और IT Rules, 2021 के Rule 4(4) का उल्लेख है।

लेकिन मुझे मूल सरकारी नोटिस या शिकायत की प्रति नहीं दी गई। किस एजेंसी ने कार्रवाई माँगी? किस पोस्ट के किस हिस्से पर आपत्ति है? ठोस कानूनी आधार क्या है? इसकी जानकारी नहीं दी गई। केवल कानून का नाम लिख देना जवाबदेही नहीं है।

प्रभावित सामग्री में 26 सितंबर का समाचार वीडियो और 16 जून की मेरे चैनल की पहचान वाली फोटो भी शामिल है। उस फोटो पर रोक क्यों?

मेरे सीधे सवाल हैं:

1. नोटिस जारी करने वाली एजेंसी का नाम, नोटिस की तारीख, संदर्भ संख्या और उसकी प्रति कहाँ है?
2. किस सामग्री का कौन-सा कथन किस कानून का उल्लंघन करता है?
3. Facebook पहले चेतावनी देने का दावा करता है। वे चेतावनियाँ कब और कहाँ भेजी गईं? उनका रिकॉर्ड दीजिए।
4. कुछ पोस्ट पर आपत्ति के आधार पर पूरे अकाउंट/पेज की पहुंच रोकने का औचित्य क्या है?
5. क्या सामग्री और उसके पत्रकारिता संबंधी संदर्भ की मानव समीक्षा हुई?
6. पहले डीमोनेटाइजेशन, शिकायत के बाद बहाली और अब यह रोक—क्या इन अलग-अलग कार्रवाइयों की पारदर्शी समीक्षा होगी?

Facebook justifies these actions by citing notices from the “Government of India/law enforcement agencies” and local laws. The notifications reference Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act and Rule 4(4) of the IT Rules, 2021.

However, I have not been provided with a copy of the original government notice or the complaint. Which agency requested this action? Which specific part of which post is being objected to? What is the concrete legal basis for this? None of this information has been shared. Simply citing a law does not constitute accountability.

The affected content includes a news video from September 26 and a photo identifying my channel, dated June 16. Why is that photo being blocked?

I have a few direct questions:

1. What is the name of the agency that issued the notice? What is the date of the notice, the reference number, and where is the copy of it?
2. Which specific statement within the content violates which law?
3. Facebook claims to provide prior warnings. When and where were these warnings sent? Please provide a record of them.
4. What is the justification for blocking access to the entire account/page based on objections to only a few posts?
5. Was there a human review of the content, taking into account its journalistic context?
6. Given the sequence of events—initial demonetization, restoration following a complaint, and now this block—will there be a transparent review of these separate actions?
7. What, exactly, will be restored after seven days? What is the path to an effective appeal?

I am not claiming that there is a common reason linking these two actions. However, such recurring actions have a direct impact on my journalism, my livelihood, and my reach to my audience.

Independent journalism cannot be left at the mercy of vague messages and opaque decisions. I demand that the original notices and clear reasons be provided, that an immediate human review be conducted, and that access to my account/page be restored.

Ministry of Electronics and IT has begun discussions on stripping social media platforms of safe harbour under Section 79 of the IT Act, 2000. Nobody should mistake this for a move against Big Tech for it is a move against the people who use these platforms.

Safe harbour is not a gift to Meta, Google or X. It is the legal foundation that lets ordinary Indians speak online without a platform's lawyers deciding in advance whether their post is worth the risk and taking it down. If it is taken away, and every platform becomes liable for every post, comment and video. The rational response for any company is to remove anything that might draw a complaint, a notice or a summons. Criticism of the government, reporting on protests, satire, and the speech of people without lawyers will be the first casualties which are already being censored by automated filters implemented pursuant to the IT Rules, 2021. The Supreme Court recognised exactly this in Shreya Singhal (2015), which is why it read down Section 79(3)(b) to require a court order or a lawful government direction before platforms must act.

The timing tells its own story as the report says that MEITY’s rethink was shaped by a view within government that platform algorithms have favoured Opposition and anti-establishment narratives over official messaging, and by the role of Instagram during the student protests in July. In other words, the complaint is not that platforms host too much illegal content but it is that they host too much content the government dislikes. 

The 2023 Fact Check Unit amendment tried to make the government the arbiter of truth about itself, until the Bombay High Court struck it down. The Sahyog portal has turned Section 79(3)(b) into a parallel, opaque takedown channel that sidesteps the safeguards of Section 69A, a practice X is now challenging in court. In August, a Parliamentary Standing Committee gave Mark Zuckerberg three days to apologise personally for the brief removal of the Prime Minister's video or face the loss of safe harbour. 

Subsequently advisories were issued on October 8, 2026 and October 10, 2026 pressuring digital platforms to implement pro-active censorship through, “enhanced due diligence”. Safe harbour was never meant to be a bargaining chip that MEITY waves at a company to extract compliance. 

There are real problems on these platforms such as child sexual abuse material, non-consensual intimate imagery and deepfakes. The Supreme Court's observations in Just Rights for Children Alliance on October 15 deserve a serious answer. But the answer is targeted, rights-respecting obligations with independent oversight, transparency about takedowns, and a grievance process that works for users. It is not a liability regime that pushes platforms to delete first and never ask. Nor is it a rule that platforms must clear product changes with the government before shipping them, which would hand the state a license raj over the design of the services Indians use every day.

Any change of this scale must go through Parliament, with a published draft, a genuine consultation and a full debate. It cannot be settled in closed-door meetings between the Ministry and a handful of companies.

IFF will send a detailed representation to the Ministry of Electronics and IT setting out why the proposed changes to Section 79 are unconstitutional and unworkable, and what a rights-respecting approach to platform accountability should look like. We will also write to the Parliamentary Standing Committee on Communications and Information Technology.

We are filing RTI applications with MeitY seeking the minutes, agendas, attendance lists and file notings of every meeting held on the review of safe harbour, including the meetings with Meta and other platforms in July and August, and the basis for the Ministry's assessment of how platform algorithms treat government and Opposition content

The Delhi High Court has in its judgement of ABD Maestro Limited v. Great Galleon Ventured Limited ruled on an aspect of law that has concerned many who have appeared for defendants over years. In a common judgment of 3 November 2026 covering seventeen commercial suits, Justice Purushaindra Kumar Kaurav returned every plaint for want of territorial jurisdiction. In more than half, neither party was in Delhi.

For instance consider the hypothetical that a plaintiff in Mumbai sues a defendant in Jodhpur, pleads a trap purchase delivered to a Delhi address, adds a line about a website being “accessible” here, and asks for an ex parte injunction. The judgment notes that the same order could have been placed from “Ladakh, Tamil Nadu, Arunachal Pradesh, or Gujarat,” and that reading the CPC to reward it makes “a mockery of the concept of territoriality.” In one suit the order was placed by the filing advocate, to the address on his vakalatnama.

What I really value in the judgement is the candour with which it approached filing practices. The Court admits that after “enjoying, effectively, a pan-India jurisdiction, it becomes difficult for a court today to draw a Lakshman Rekha,” and describes itself as a Banyan Tree that “also stunts the growth of other trees below it.” It calls investigator-led trap orders “gaming of the system,” refuses to be a “silent spectator in this theatre called ‘jurisdiction’ scripted by the plaintiff,” and records a plaintiff who, asked for the basis of its pleading, “roars ‘demurrer doctrine’.”

The real problem has always been the summons stage. Jurisdiction paragraphs in IP plaints were in the past not put to sufficient scrutiny on the first date, the injunction issued, and the objection left for the defendant to raise months later at its own cost. That laxity made the High Court a magnet for IP litigation which often went beyond territoriality. I am pasting some tables (can post only 4 images) from the judgement (another really cool addition that makes the application of principles under it clear) which I have skimmed but hopefully will read more deeply in the coming days.

text: Amnesty International India stands in solidarity with the Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF), Software Freedom Law Center (SFLC) and geoblockedindia, whose work documenting internet censorship and defending digital rights is now being targeted through police notices seeking the removal of their social media accounts and posts.  The attempt to silence organizations and social media accounts for documenting censorship is deeply alarming. It threatens not only their freedom of expression but also the public's right to know when, why and how access to information is being restricted.  Those who expose censorship must not become its targets.

The Delhi Police has asked X to take down @internetfreedom account, six of its posts, the accounts of @SFLCin and @geoblockedindia, and posts by 16 other users, alleging that the content defames the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS).  The posts in question document and comment on a legal notice said to be sent in the RSS's name to these three organizations, demanding that they stop criticizing and documenting government blocking orders.  This raises serious concerns about the use of state power to suppress public scrutiny of internet censorship and discourage legitimate criticism.

IFF works to defend digital rights and in the past three weeks assisted 86 people whose accounts were suspended or whose posts were withheld in India. SFLC documents restrictions on online expression and geoblockedindia publishes blocking orders when platforms disclose them.  Journalists, civil society organizations and independent researchers must be able to scrutinize government action, document restrictions and seek legal remedies without fear of intimidation or retaliation.  Transparency about censorship cannot itself be treated as an offense.

*STATEMENT: Escalating Digital Censorship in India*

*New Delhi, February 28, 2026*

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) is concerned by a cluster of online blocking and takedown actions and ISP level service disruptions reported between 24–28 February 2026. Across these incidents, users and affected services face restrictions without clear, timely reasons and without access to the underlying orders needed to challenge state action by exercising their rights to obtain legal remedy.

Developers reported severe, uneven disruption in access to Supabase across multiple Indian networks. Reporting indicates the disruption followed a government direction, with accounts suggesting use of Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000. Yet there has been no public statement of the grounds, scope, or duration, and no accessible order for those impacted. Supabase has publicly stated that its domains became inaccessible due to a “ministry order”, and users have been pushed to workarounds such as alternative DNS or VPNs. In parallel, users on X (formerly Twitter) continue to receive “withheld in India” notices restricting specific posts within the country. Such notices usually do not provide the government order or its reasoning. Hence, for those who are being censored the basics of natural justice of a notice, opportunity for a hearing and remedy are delayed or absent.

This is enabled by secrecy built into the blocking framework. Section 69A is implemented through the 2009 Blocking Rules, which contemplate a committee process and, where feasible, notice to intermediaries and identifiable originators. But they also impose “strict confidentiality” over requests and actions taken. When orders and reasons are secret by default, affected persons cannot test legality, necessity, proportionality, or factual errors except through protracted litigation. When in _Shreya Singhal v. Union of India_ (2015), the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A while relying on the existence of procedural safeguards and reasoned decisions, indicating that impacted users could approach court in writ remedies. However, due to the operational secrecy and providing copies of orders and notices those who are censored and prevented from obtaining judicial remedy.

The February 2026 amendments to the IT Rules, 2021 further increase these risks. The substituted Rule 3(1)(d) requires intermediaries to remove or disable access within three hours of receiving “actual knowledge”, which can arise from a court order or a written “reasoned intimation” by authorised government officers. While the rule lists what a “reasoned intimation” should contain, the legal basis, statutory provision, nature of the unlawful act, and specific URL/identifier, the three-hour window pressures platforms to comply promptly which may often occur without any substantive assessment. These inherently opaque censorship practices are being accelerated through "Sahyog" portal. Developed by the Indian Cybercrime Coordination Centre (I4C), the Sahyog portal operates entirely without statutory footing, only being anchored in the IT Rules, 2021 that are created by executive notification. It functions as a censorship clearinghouse that deliberately bypasses the established, albeit weak, procedural safeguards of Section 69A. By routing automated takedown directives directly to intermediaries under Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act, the portal structurally excludes citizens and impacted users from the grievance process.

We demand that the government introduce strictly judicially enforceable transparency requirements, publish all blocking orders, and restore the principles of natural justice to India's platform governance framework. Based on requests from our community we will also next week launch a rough public sheet in which social media users can input and add information on digital censorship.

PUBLIC STATEMENT BY PARANJOY GUHA THAKURTA
On the arbitrary takedown of https://t.co/TMPhYqaVhe by Hostinger following legal notices from Indiabulls founder Sameer Gehlaut
October 31, 2026
On the morning of October 28, 2026, my website https://t.co/OeAAoTPXCy and all its associated subdomains, including https://t.co/I8kylhDXVk and https://t.co/D8b6LtNzWD, were abruptly taken offline by our web hosting provider, Hostinger (HOSTINGER operations, UAB). The website, registered twelve years ago, serves as an online archive of my work over several decades as a journalist, author, publisher, and maker of documentary films and music videos
Hostinger gave no prior intimation, warning, or opportunity to respond before suspending the entire hosting account. When my colleague contacted Hostinger “Support” at 6:48 AM on October 28, a hosting “specialist” stated that the suspension was triggered by an abuse report for "Fraud/Scam" and declared that "unsuspension is not negotiable in this case."
This sudden shutdown of an entire repository under the label "Fraud/Scam" happened just days after Sameer Gehlaut, founder of the Indiabulls group, served me with an ex parte court order demanding the removal of a single article published more than seven years on https://t.co/25noyNupwJ.
For over six years, Indiabulls and Shri Gehlaut have pursued legal action over this report and I have consistently defended our journalistic report in court. Here is the timeline:
·  March 11, 2020: Indiabulls Housing Finance Limited filed a criminal defamation complaint (CC No. 1765/2020) before the Patiala House Courts, New Delhi, against NewsClick, its Reader's Editor Urmilesh, co-author of the article Sourodipto Sanyal, NewsClick editor Prabir Purkayastha, and me over an article published on the website on September 30, 2019.
·  June 6, 2025 and July 9, 2025: More than five years after the complaint was filed, a Judicial Magistrate at Patiala House Courts passed an order on June 6, 2025, dropping proceedings against Shri Purkayastha while issuing summons to the remaining four accused, including me, under Sections 499 and 500 of the Indian Penal Code. A formal summons was issued on July 9, 2025, for appearance on July 30, 2025.
·  August 27, 2026: Counsel for Shri Gehlaut, sent me a legal notice demanding the takedown of the article within 24 to 48 hours, claiming that a status report by the Economic Offences Wing (EOW) of the Delhi Police had altered the factual position.
·  September 2, 2026: My counsel sent a reply pointing out concerns with the legal notice
·  October 24, 2026: Indiabulls Nests Limited (Plaintiff No. 1) and Sameer Gehlaut (Plaintiff No. 2) obtained an ex parte ad interim injunction from the Court of one of the District and Sessions Judges, Patiala House Courts, New Delhi, in Civil Suit No. 529/2026 (Indiabulls Nests Ltd. & Anr. v. Ashok Kumar/John Doe & Ors.), in which I am arrayed as Defendant No. 19. The order directed the removal and de-indexing of the article on https://t.co/TMPhYqaVhe (listed as Item A-33 in Schedule A).
·  October 25, 2026 (10:13 AM IST): Advocates representing Indiabulls Nests Limited and Sameer Gehlaut, emailed me the October 24 court order and suit documents, demanding immediate deletion and written confirmation of compliance.
·  October 26, 2026 (11:33 PM IST): Sameer Gehlaut personally sent an email from his official address (sameer@indiabulls.com) demanding the immediate deletion of the URL from https://t.co/TMPhYqaVhe and threatening to move the court under Order XXXIX Rule 2A of the Code of Civil Procedure if I did not comply, noting that the matter is next listed on December 18, 2026. While I was in the process of challenging the order dated 24.10.2026 before higher forums, on the same day, advocates representing Shri Gehlaut submitted a court order takedown complaint to Google LLC.

·  October 28, 2026 (3:16 PM IST): Google Search Console sent an automated notice ([WNC-598900]) informing me that Google was blocking the specific URL https://t.co/SsSVUVLKGX  from appearing in search results on https://t.co/2IOZ4I1WqC.

The Lumen Database record of this complaint (Notice ID: 101001876) reveals the scale of the takedown request. The complaint targeted 52 URLs on websites across major national and international news organisations, including The Economic Times, Business Standard, The Caravan, The Daily Pioneer, Business Today, Deccan Herald, ET Now, Financial Express, Livemint, Moneycontrol, Moneylife, NDTV Profit, The New Indian Express, Outlook Business, The Quint, Quartz, and NewsClick, along with posts on X (formerly Twitter), Facebook, Instagram, LinkedIn, and Scribd.

Most of these reports on major corporate news websites remain accessible online. In fact, Item 39 on the Lumen takedown list is the original September 30, 2019 article published on https://t.co/qQP2N2fxA2: https://t.co/hgneAPvDuF, which remains live and accessible  as of now.

Yet, in the case of https://t.co/TMPhYqaVhe, the entire domain and every website hosted on my account were wiped off the internet.

Hostinger's Baseless "Fraud/Scam" Claim and Demand for Accountability

Hostinger did not cite the Patiala House Courts order when it suspended my account on October 28, 2026. Instead, its representative claimed that the hosting account was permanently suspended due to an abuse report for "Fraud/Scam".

This allegation is demonstrably false:

1. VirusTotal Security Analysis: Independent domain checks conducted on October 28, 2026, at 7:48 AM and 7:54 AM on VirusTotal confirm that 0 out of 92 security vendors flagged https://t.co/TMPhYqaVhe or https://t.co/I8kylhDXVk as malicious, phishing, or fraudulent. VirusTotal explicitly categorises https://t.co/TMPhYqaVhe under "news and media".

2. Google Safe Browsing Status: Checks on the Google Safe Browsing diagnostic tool at 7:55 AM and 7:56 AM on October 28, 2026, for both https://t.co/TMPhYqaVhe and https://t.co/D8b6LtNzWD returned the status: "No unsafe content found".
My website https://t.co/OeAAoTPXCy does not sell financial products, solicit funds for commercial schemes, or engage in any activity that could remotely be classified as a scam. It is a repository of public-interest journalism, books, documentary films, and investigative reports built over a lifetime of work. By acting on a fabricated "Fraud/Scam" abuse report without a single verification check or prior notice to the domain owner, Hostinger has allowed its abuse-reporting mechanism to be weaponised to censor an independent journalist.
Even where a court order directs the removal or de-indexing of a specific URL, a web hosting provider has no legal or ethical justification to pull down an entire domain and hundreds of unrelated articles, archives, and subdomains without notice.
I demand immediate answers and accountability from Hostinger:
1. Who submitted the false "Fraud/Scam" abuse report against https://t.co/TMPhYqaVhe, and on what exact date and time was it received?
2. What internal verification did Hostinger's abuse team conduct before classifying a 12-year-old journalism portal as a "Fraud/Scam" site, especially when 92 security vendors on VirusTotal and Google Safe Browsing show zero malicious or unsafe content?
3. Why was no prior notice, warning, or copy of the complaint sent to me before suspending the entire hosting account?
4. On what basis did Hostinger's specialist declare that the suspension of an entire archive of journalistic work is "not negotiable"?
While my legal advisers are in the process of taking appropriate steps in court regarding the ex parte order dated October 24, 2026, and the wholesale suspension of my website, this backdoor censorship through web hosting providers sets a dangerous precedent for the independence of the media and freedom of expression as enshrined in Article (19)(1)(a) of the Constitution of India as a fundamental right of every citizen of India.
Yours sincerely

Paranjoy Guha Thakurta
Independent Journalist, Author, Publisher and Maker of Documentary Films and Music Videos
